claim.why_it_matters: Two members of one numbered series sit two heading levels above their five siblings purely because a page break fell between them. The outline then shows ACCEPT FROM DAY-OF-WEEK and ACCEPT FROM TIME as top-level annex clauses rather than as parts of D.31.2, which is exactly the kind of drift that makes a section-anchored citation resolve to the wrong scope.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED as filed. Nothing is missing and no content differs; the only difference is markdown '#' depth, and the claim misstates both its magnitude and its consequence. (1) NOTHING IS MISSING. The filed kind is 'missing-heading', but both headings are present in the transcription with the correct clause number and the correct title, verbatim against the render: page-1194.md line 7 '## D.31.2.6 ACCEPT FROM DAY-OF-WEEK' and line 12 '## D.31.2.7 ACCEPT FROM TIME'. The PDF (E:/Temp/specrecon/v1194/spec_p1194.png) prints exactly those two headings, and both bodies transcribe faithfully -- the one-digit DAY-OF-WEEK text (1=Monday … 7=Sunday; for example, 3), the eight-digit TIME text (00-23 / 00-59 / 00-59 / hundredths; for example, 05142781), and the LEAP-SECOND directive paragraph. Not one word of normative content is lost, altered, or reflowed away. (2) THE MAGNITUDE IS MISQUOTED. The claim says the two headings 'sit two heading levels above their five siblings'. The claim's own quoted strings show '##' versus '###' -- that is ONE level, not two. Verified in specs/ISO_COBOL.md: D.31.2.1-D.31.2.5 are '###' (lines 48178-48198), D.31.2.6-D.31.2.7 are '##' (lines 48210, 48215). (3) THE STATED HARM IS FALSE. The claim asserts this 'makes a section-anchored citation resolve to the wrong scope'. It does not. Citations in this repo resolve by the explicit anchor, and both anchors are present and correct immediately above their headings: '' and ''. A cite of D.31.2.6 lands on D.31.2.6. Clause rank in ISO/IEC 1989:2023 is carried by the printed dotted number, not by typography, and the numbers 'D.31.2.6' / 'D.31.2.7' are intact in the markdown -- so the parent-child relationship to D.31.2 is still unambiguously readable. (4) THE PDF ITSELF DOES NOT TYPOGRAPHICALLY DISTINGUISH THESE RANKS. I compared the two renders directly. On page 1193 the PDF prints 'D.31.2 Temporal format ACCEPT statement' (3-component) and 'D.31.2.1 General' … 'D.31.2.5 ACCEPT FROM DAY YYYYDDD' (4-component) in the SAME bold face, at the SAME point size, at the SAME left margin. Page 1194 prints D.31.2.6, D.31.2.7, D.31.3 and D.31.3.1 in that identical style as well. So the PDF supplies no visual rank signal to have been 'lost' -- the transcriber's '##' vs '###' choice is an interpretation layered on top of the source, and the source's actual rank signal (the number) survives intact. (5) IT IS A SYSTEMIC PAGINATION ARTIFACT, NOT A PAGE-1194 DEFECT. Walking heading levels against page anchors across D.31 shows a mechanical rule: a 4-component subclause is '###' when it starts on the SAME page as its 3-component parent heading, and '##' when it starts on a later page. D.31.3.1-.2 sit on page 1194 with parent D.31.3 -> '###'; D.31.3.3-.9 spill to page 1195 -> '##'. D.31.4.1-.5 all fit on page 1196 with parent D.31.4 -> all '###'. D.31.5.1 sits on 1196 with D.31.5 -> '###'; D.31.5.2-.11 spill to 1197-1199 -> '##'. This is per-page transcription furniture reproduced dozens of times, i.e. exactly the 'page-break furniture / formatting' class the verification criteria direct me to reject, and it is in no way specific to the D.31.2.6/D.31.2.7 pair the claim singles out. Bottom line: a genuine but purely cosmetic markdown-depth inconsistency exists; it is not a content discrepancy, nothing is missing, meaning is unchanged, and citation resolution is unaffected. Filing it as a structural 'missing-heading' overstates it on every axis.
verdict.corrected_description: Cosmetic markup-depth inconsistency only -- NOT a content discrepancy, and not 'missing'. Both headings are present and verbatim correct ('D.31.2.6 ACCEPT FROM DAY-OF-WEEK', 'D.31.2.7 ACCEPT FROM TIME'), both bodies transcribe faithfully, and both carry correct anchors (section-d-31-2-6, section-d-31-2-7) so citations resolve to the right scope. The only difference is that the markdown writes these two 4-component subclauses as '##' while their siblings D.31.2.1-.5 are '###' -- a ONE-level gap, not two. The PDF gives no typographic rank cue to lose: on the renders of pages 1193 and 1194 the 3-component headings (D.31.2, D.31.3) and the 4-component headings (D.31.2.1-.7, D.31.3.1-.2) are printed in identical bold face, size and indent; rank is conveyed solely by the dotted number, which the markdown preserves. The demotion is a mechanical pagination artifact applied throughout the annex -- a 4-component subclause gets '###' only when it begins on the same page as its parent heading and '##' otherwise (D.31.3.3-.9 on p1195, D.31.5.2-.11 on p1197-1199 are all likewise '##', while D.31.4.1-.5, which share p1196 with D.31.4, are all '###'). If anyone wants this normalized it is a global heading-depth pass over the transcription, not a page-1194 spec-fidelity fix.
